title.value: Dementia prevention, intervention, and care: 2020 report of the Lancet Commission
title.quote: Dementia prevention, intervention, and care: 2020 report of the Lancet Commission

design.value: Commission evidence synthesis: a reconvened expert Commission using a triangulation framework, presenting a narrative synthesis of existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses and performing new systematic literature reviews and meta-analyses (for excessive alcohol consumption and traumatic brain injury) to build an updated 12 risk factor life-course model and population attributable fraction (PAF) calculation
design.quote: Within this framework, we present a narrative synthesis of evidence including systematic reviews and meta-analyses and explain its balance, strengths, and limitations.

n_description.value: The report states no single headline N of its own. Its new PAF calculation drew communality (risk-factor clustering) from a representative sample of over 10 000 UK community-dwelling adults, covering 11 of the 12 risk factors; the risk factor relative risks come from separately reported meta-analyses and cohort studies.
n_description.quote: We used a representative sample of over 10 000 UK community-dwelling adults, to calculate communality (clustering of risk factors) of 11 risk factors for which data existed, to allow calculation of each factor's unique risk.

population.value: The worldwide population at risk of dementia, modelled with global risk factor figures; the report states that nearly all the underlying evidence comes from studies in high-income countries
population.quote: Nearly all the evidence is from studies in high-income countries (HIC), so risks might differ in other countries and interventions might require modification for different cultures and environments.

outcomes.name: New random-effects meta-analysis: relative risk of all-cause dementia for drinking more than 21 units of alcohol weekly in midlife, versus lighter drinking (analysis performed by the Commission)
outcomes.prespecification_evidence: We used inclusion criteria: original population-based cohort studies measuring drinking during midlife, as alcohol intake tends to fall with age
outcomes.effect_estimate: RR 1·18; three studies met the inclusion criteria; weighted PAF 0·8
outcomes.quote: The RR associated with drinking—more than 21 units (168 g) of alcohol weekly—compared with lighter drinking was 1·18 (95% Cl 1·06–1·31; ).
outcomes.location: Incorporation of the new chosen risks in new systematic reviews, Alcohol

outcomes.name: New random-effects meta-analysis: pooled relative risk of all-cause dementia from traumatic brain injury of all severities (analysis performed by the Commission)
outcomes.prespecification_evidence: We used inclusion criteria: original population-based cohort studies, baseline TBI of all severities reported, and all-cause dementia ascertained at follow-up using validated clinical measures.
outcomes.effect_estimate: pooled RR 1·84 for all cause dementia from all severities of TBI, with heterogeneity in study-specific estimates; TBI adult population prevalence 12·1%; weighted PAF 3·4
outcomes.quote: The pooled RR was 1·84 (95% CI 1·54–2·20) for all cause dementia from all severities of TBI ( ) although there was heterogeneity in study-specific estimates, possibly because of different populations.
outcomes.location: Incorporation of the new chosen risks in new systematic reviews, TBI

outcomes.name: Relative risk of dementia for air pollution exposure, three highest quartiles versus lowest quartile, taken from a single Canadian cohort because meta-analysis was not possible
outcomes.prespecification_evidence: We included longitudinal studies with assessment of all cause air pollution exposure; use of formal assessment of cognitive function at baseline; report of incident all-cause dementia, data from adults (age ≥18 years); and a minimum follow-up of 6 months.
outcomes.effect_estimate: RR 1·09 for those in the three highest quartiles of air pollution exposure compared to the lowest
outcomes.quote: We calculated the RR of dementia for those in the three highest quartiles compared to the lowest was 1·09 (1·07–1·11).
outcomes.location: Incorporation of the new chosen risks in new systematic reviews, Pollution

outcomes.name: Attributable fraction of dementia for exposure to the highest three quartiles versus the lowest quartile of PM 2·5 and NO 2, and the weighted PAF carried into the 12 factor model
outcomes.quote: The attributable fraction for exposure to the highest three quartiles versus the lowest quartile of PM 2·5 and NO 2 was 6·1% (4·8–7·5). The weighted PAF was 2·3.
outcomes.location: Incorporation of the new chosen risks in new systematic reviews, Pollution

primary_endpoint_status.explanation: This is a Commission evidence synthesis with no endpoint of its own: it reports modelled population attributable fractions built from reviewed observational evidence under an assumption of causation, not a tested endpoint with a prespecified success threshold.
primary_endpoint_status.quote: We performed systematic literature reviews and meta-analyses where needed to generate new evidence for our analysis of potentially modifiable risk factors for dementia.

limitations: Together the 12 modifiable risk factors account for around 40% of worldwide dementias, which consequently could theoretically be prevented or delayed.
We have made assumptions to calculate this new model.
We have assumed a causal relationship between risk factors and dementia, although we have been cautious and not included risk factors with less good evidence.

Association does not prove causation, however, as already noted, the reductions in prevalence and incidence in several HIC suggests that at least some of the risk factors estimated here do have a causal relationship with the clinical expression of dementia.
Although behaviour change is difficult and some associations might not be purely causal, individuals have a huge potential to reduce their dementia risk.

We used global figures for dementia risk although we know the risk factors prevalence varies between countries and most global research is from HIC, so LMIC are under-represented because of lack of data.
Nearly all the evidence is from studies in high-income countries (HIC), so risks might differ in other countries and interventions might require modification for different cultures and environments.
No single database exists with all 12 risk factors together, but we found 11 of the factors in a UK database and used the mean figure for communality calculations for TBI.
We do not know how far findings of communality in other geographical populations might differ, or in those with a differing distribution of age groups or sex.
We found that social isolation was not explicitly measured and had to use proxies, such as cohabitation when considering prevalence, which are approximate.

We were also unable to meta-analyse data on pollution and thus unlike the other relative risks, the figure comes from only one study, from an area of low pollution so is likely to be an underestimate.
Specifically, evidence for the association of alcohol misuse with dementia comes from HIC and future studies from LMIC are needed to complete the picture.
Risk factors might also matter more at a time of higher biological vulnerability, which the studies we have drawn on cannot establish.

The length of exposure required for risk or protection effect, and their inter-relationships as they change across life is unclear—it seems probable that longer or more intense exposure has stronger effects.
Additionally, as our communality figures show, risk factors overlap. We cannot establish from these data if having multiple risk factors has an additive or synergistic effect.
When measuring a risk nearer to the age of dementia onset, then it is more likely that prodromal change affects, or even causes it.
Data from RCTs on interventions to prevent cognitive decline, all-cause dementia, or Alzheimer's disease are few.
Although we have more to learn about effectiveness, avoiding or delaying even a proportion of potentially modifiable dementias should be a national priority for all.

risk_of_bias.domain: modelled estimate rather than demonstrated prevention (assumption of causation)
risk_of_bias.judgement: The 40% headline is a population attributable fraction calculated under an explicit assumption that the risk factor associations are causal; the report itself frames the resulting prevention as theoretical, not demonstrated by intervention
risk_of_bias.quote: We have assumed a causal relationship between risk factors and dementia, although we have been cautious and not included risk factors with less good evidence.

risk_of_bias.domain: absence of randomised evidence for the modelled preventive effect
risk_of_bias.judgement: The report states that trial data on interventions to prevent dementia are few, so the PAF model is built almost entirely on observational associations
risk_of_bias.quote: Data from RCTs on interventions to prevent cognitive decline, all-cause dementia, or Alzheimer's disease are few.

risk_of_bias.judgement: For several late-life risk factors the report states the direction of effect cannot be resolved; inactivity and depression may be consequences of prodromal dementia
risk_of_bias.quote: People might stop exercising due to prodromal dementia so inactivity might be either a consequence or a cause or both in dementia and might be more of a risk in those with cardiovascular morbidity.

risk_of_bias.judgement: Two of the 12 risk factors were represented in the PAF calculation by proxies rather than direct measures
risk_of_bias.quote: We used cohabitation as a proxy measure for social contact, and urbanicity for air pollution exposure.

risk_of_bias.domain: overlap and non-independence of risk factors (communality)
risk_of_bias.judgement: The 12 risk factors are substantially correlated, which the report handles by weighting for communality; its own analysis found substantial overlap and the communality of TBI could not be measured at all
risk_of_bias.quote: Our analysis found four principal components, explaining 55% of the total variance between the eleven risk factors, suggesting substantial overlap.

risk_of_bias.domain: single-study basis for the air pollution estimate
risk_of_bias.judgement: The air pollution relative risk rests on one Canadian cohort from a low-pollution setting, without meta-analysis
risk_of_bias.quote: As meta-analysis was not possible, we used data from the only study of all-cause air pollution with the outcome of all-cause dementia, with low-moderate risk of bias.

risk_of_bias.judgement: The report acknowledges that raised dementia risk from air pollutants remains open to residual confounding, particularly its entanglement with poverty and deprivation
risk_of_bias.quote: Although the higher levels of dementia from air pollutants are still subject to the potential for residual confounding, the effects on animal models are evidence of physiological effects over and above those driven by life-course deprivation.

risk_of_bias.domain: geographical generalisability of the global estimate
risk_of_bias.judgement: Global PAF figures are derived predominantly from high-income country data, with LMIC under-represented despite the report claiming higher preventive potential there
risk_of_bias.quote: We used global figures for dementia risk although we know the risk factors prevalence varies between countries and most global research is from HIC, so LMIC are under-represented because of lack of data.

risk_of_bias.judgement: Several Commission members declare grants and personal fees from companies developing dementia therapeutics, including one grant reported as during the conduct of the study
risk_of_bias.quote: DA reports grants from Eli Lilly, during the conduct of the study.

disagreements.question: Is the 40% figure a demonstrated preventive effect or a modelled estimate?
disagreements.position: The Commission presents 40% as a modelled population attributable fraction computed under an assumption of causation, describing the associated dementias as ones that could theoretically be prevented or delayed rather than as prevention already shown
disagreements.attributed_to: 2020 report of the Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, intervention, and care
disagreements.quote: Together the 12 modifiable risk factors account for around 40% of worldwide dementias, which consequently could theoretically be prevented or delayed.

disagreements.question: Do amyloid and tau biomarkers support pre-symptomatic diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease in everyday practice?
disagreements.position: No; the Commission states that most cognitively normal people with only these biomarkers never develop the disease and that no evidence supports pre-symptomatic diagnosis in everyday practice
disagreements.attributed_to: 2020 report of the Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, intervention, and care
disagreements.quote: Amyloid-β and tau biomarkers indicate risk of progression to Alzheimer's dementia but most people with normal cognition with only these biomarkers never develop the disease.

disagreements.question: Can prognosis be given to an individual on the basis of amyloid or tau biomarkers?
disagreements.position: No; the Commission holds that individual-level prognostication is not possible because most cognitively normal people with these markers do not develop dementia in a clinically relevant timeframe
disagreements.attributed_to: 2020 report of the Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, intervention, and care
disagreements.quote: at the individual level prognostication is not possible as most cognitively normal people with these markers do not develop dementia within a clinically relevant timeframe

disagreements.question: Should vitamins, oils or dietary supplements be used to prevent dementia?
disagreements.position: No; the Commission recommends against them because extensive trial testing has produced no signals of benefit
disagreements.attributed_to: 2020 report of the Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, intervention, and care
disagreements.quote: We do not recommend taking additional vitamins, oils, or mixed dietary supplements as a means of preventing dementia as extensive testing in trials has not led to signals of beneficial effects.

disagreements.question: Do statins prevent cognitive decline or dementia in older people at vascular risk?
disagreements.position: No; the Commission reports a Cochrane review finding good evidence that they do not
disagreements.attributed_to: Cochrane review, as cited by the Lancet Commission
disagreements.quote: A Cochrane review reported good evidence that statins given to older people at risk of vascular disease do not prevent cognitive decline or dementia.

disagreements.question: Does intensive glycaemic control reduce dementia risk in type 2 diabetes?
disagreements.position: No; the Commission states plainly that intensive diabetic control does not decrease the risk of dementia, while maintaining that diabetes itself is a clear risk factor
disagreements.attributed_to: 2020 report of the Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, intervention, and care
disagreements.quote: Overall type 2 diabetes is a clear risk factor for development of future dementia; however, whether any particular medication ameliorates this risk is unclear. Intensive diabetic control does not decrease the risk of dementia.

disagreements.question: Has anti-amyloid drug development produced advances by 2020?
disagreements.position: No; the Commission reports no advances in amyloid-beta therapeutics and negative phase 3 results for monoclonal antibodies and beta-secretase inhibitors
disagreements.attributed_to: 2020 report of the Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, intervention, and care
disagreements.quote: No advances have been reported in Aβ therapeutics, with negative results from phase 3 trials of monoclonal antibodies (eg, solanezumab, crenezumab) and inhibitors of β-secretase, a protease involved in the production of Aβ peptides.

disagreements.question: Which preventive medication has established effect on dementia?
disagreements.position: Only antihypertensive treatment for hypertension; the Commission names it as the sole known effective preventive medication for dementia
disagreements.attributed_to: 2020 report of the Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, intervention, and care
disagreements.quote: Aim to maintain systolic BP of 130 mm Hg or less in midlife from around age 40 years (antihypertensive treatment for hypertension is the only known effective preventive medication for dementia).
